report.source_text: A decision was made to perform angiographic coiling of the SAA. The femoral artery on the right side was punctured to establish vascular access for embolization. Following the identification of the SAA, fibered angiocoils of different sizes along with 2 ml of lipiodol were utilised as the embolisation material. Lipiodol, an iodine-based embolisation material, helped to delineate the vessel architecture better. The procedure was considered successful upon visual confirmation of thrombosis within the SAA.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 31-year-old woman with known Child's B liver cirrhosis, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and initial low WBC (1.9 x 10^9 cells/L) and platelet counts (54 x 10^9 cells/L) presented with a one-month history of dull left hypochondriac abdominal pain. Diagnostic workup with a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a saccular-type splenic artery aneurysm (SAA) measuring 3.4 x 3.4 x 4.3 cm with thrombus and splenic infarction (E001). The SAA was successfully treated with angiographic coiling, confirmed by visual thrombosis during the procedure (E002) and by a follow-up CT angiogram showing a thrombosed splenic artery (E003). Post-embolization, the patient showed significant improvement in blood counts, with WBC increasing to 5.0 x 10^9 cells/L and platelet counts to 209 x 10^9 cells/L (E004). A follow-up CT also demonstrated a reduction in spleen size from 10.8 x 7.4 x 18.6 cm to 9.3 x 5.4 x 16.1 cm (E005). This clinical course supports the diagnosis of SAA as the cause of abdominal pain and hypersplenism, which improved after SAA treatment, all in the context of underlying liver cirrhosis.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a saccular-type splenic artery aneurysm (SAA) at the mid to distal splenic artery measuring 3.4 x 3.4 x 4.3 cm with thrombus and splenic infarction.
